name: Nyoro
confidence_why: Kaji (2010, 2021) describes Nyoro from his own fieldwork as a two-pattern tone language (one high tone per word, on the penultimate or the final syllable, no all-low words) and Yukawa (2002) independently transcribes the same pitch contrasts in verbs, while Kaji's earlier (2006) guess that Nyoro might have lost tone was made before he had Nyoro data and is withdrawn by his own later descriptions.

catalog_quote: In general, Nyoro nouns include two underlying tone patterns: they are either penultimate high or ultimate high, regardless of the number of syllables that constitute words (…σσ́σ, …σσσ́). It is also important to note that there are no entirely low-toned words (…σσσ). The tone bearing unit is the syllable, and both short and long vowels and diphthongs behave in the same manner. For the sake of reference, penultimate high-toned nouns are called “tone pattern A nouns,” while ultimate high-toned nouns are referred to as “tone pattern B nouns.” [...] Generally, in tone pattern A nouns, high tones are realized as falling in isolation. However, they are set right when the pause is eliminated, as in (2), where the possessive adjective -ánge (“my”) directly follows the head noun. [...] Tone pattern B nouns include an underlying high tone on the ultimate syllable of the word. In contrast to pattern A nouns, high tone anticipation obligatorily applies to tone pattern B nouns. Thus, the underlying high tone of pattern B nouns is realized in the following way in isolation, i.e., the high tone is copied to the left-adjacent syllable and leaves its trace as a falling tone on the original ultimate syllable. [...] Verb forms also include two tone patterns: tone pattern A and tone pattern B like nouns.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Nyoro word carries exactly one underlying High, located either on the penultimate or on the final syllable (a lexical two-way choice for nouns; no toneless words; all preceding syllables Low). Before pause a penult H surfaces as a fall (…F-L) and a final H is anticipated onto the penult and surfaces as …H-F; phrase-medially the underlying positions show (…H-L vs …H-H). Verb infinitives and most conjugated forms take the penult-H pattern; monosyllabic-root infinitives and certain TAM forms take the final-H pattern. Kaji calls this 'tone' (a two-pattern, '2型' system) while noting it is debatable whether such a language is a tone language; nothing is said about stress as distinct from this H.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; all syllables before the final two are Low.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic (-CV-) verb infinitives take final H (okúlyâ 'to eat') whereas all other infinitives take penult H (Kaji 2018: 192; Kaji 2021 ILCAA fn.9); verb TAM forms select pattern A or B grammatically and nine affirmative tenses undergo High Tone Deletion (Kaji 2021 KSU 54).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level underlying H; citation (pre-pausal) forms differ from phrase-medial forms: isolation A = …FL, B = …HF; before a following word A = …HL, B = …HH (Kaji 2021 ILCAA ch.7 p.144-145, exx. (1)-(3)). Same facts stated in Japanese in the dedicated chapter: 'ニョロ語の声調言語としての特徴は、いわゆる 2 型の言語であるということである。つまり、単語を構成する音節数に関わりなく、声調のパターンは 2 つしかない。' (p.141) and '基底形では、最後 2 音節が、A 型の単語は HL、そして B 型の単語は LH となる。最後 2 音節より前はすべて L である。' (p.145).
new_statements.identity_note: All Kaji sources describe Nyoro proper (Orunyoro, JE11, fieldwork based in Hoima, Bunyoro) = nyor1246. Not to be conflated with Tooro (toor1238), the other half of the 'Runyoro-Rutooro' written standard, which Kaji describes as having lost the lexical contrast (H always on the penult in isolation). Rubongoya 1999 and Maddox 1902 treat Runyoro-Rutooro jointly.

tone_statements.quote: 本稿では声調変異をもたらす要因を詳しく考察し，ニョロ語の声調単位は音節であるが，命令形形成においてはモーラも関与することを明らかにする。 || This paper particularly explores imperative mood forms in terms of tone patterns and demonstrates that tone patterns change depending on whether the object pronoun is used or not, and if used, it is the first person singular or not. It also evinces that the mora, not the syllable, counts in deciding the tone pattern of imperatives even though the syllable is the tone bearing unit in this language.
tone_statements.translation: (ja part) This paper examines in detail the factors that cause tonal variation and shows that, although the tonal unit of Nyoro is the syllable, the mora is also involved in the formation of imperatives.

tone_statements.quote: ニョロ語の名詞類の声調は単語の長さに関係なく 2 パターンである。（3）は名詞の声調による最小対の例である。（3a）のパターンは，基底で終わりから 2 音節目に高声調 H（high）があるもの（便宜上パターン A と呼ぶ），そして（3b）のパターンは基底において最後の音節に高声調 H があるもの（便宜上パターン B と呼ぶ）である。[...] ニョロ語の動詞語根の声調パターンは 1 つで，不定形では原則パターン A で現れるが，これは動詞活用形で声調パターンがすべて A になるということではない。声調パターンが A，B のどちらになるかは，テンス・アスペクト・ムードごと，またその肯定・否定ごとに決まっている
tone_statements.translation: The tone of Nyoro nominals has two patterns regardless of word length. (3) is a tonal minimal pair of nouns: pattern (3a) has an underlying high tone H on the second syllable from the end (called pattern A for convenience), and pattern (3b) has an underlying H on the last syllable (pattern B). [...] Nyoro verb roots have a single tone pattern and infinitives in principle appear in pattern A, but this does not mean all conjugated forms are A: whether a form is A or B is fixed per tense/aspect/mood and per affirmative/negative.
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 ニョロ語の声調, pp.63-64
tone_statements.n_tones: H vs zero; two patterns (A penult H, B final H)

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about Nyoro among sources actually describing it. The only tension is internal to Kaji's oeuvre: the 2006 paper (p.178) speculates, explicitly without Nyoro data, that Luo contact may have led to 'tone loss in Tooro and Nyoro', whereas Kaji 2010 (ZASPiL 53, p.103) and Kaji 2021 (the catalog's existing statement) describe Nyoro as retaining two contrastive underlying tone patterns (penultimate H vs ultimate H, no all-low words; H realized falling in isolation, strong H anticipation). The 2006 remark is a superseded conjecture, not a description, so it does not count as a conflict with the catalog.

sources.note: Dedicated 22-page description: Nyoro is a '2型' (two-pattern) system - whatever the syllable count, the last two syllables are either FL (underlying..HL, 'A型') or HF (underlying..LH, 'B型'), everything before is L (p.141, 143-145); minimal pairs (p.142-3); author notes it is debatable whether such a language should be called a tone language but uses 'tone' (p.141); verb infinitives all A-type except monosyllabic verbs; summary (39) p.160. tone.quote: ニョロ語の名詞類の声調は単語の長さに関係なく 2 パターンである。（3）は名詞の声調による最小対の例である。（3a）のパターンは，基底で終わりから 2 音節目に高声調 H（high）があるもの（便宜上パターン A と呼ぶ），そして（3b）のパターンは基底において最後の音節に高声調 H があるもの（便宜上パターン B と呼ぶ）である。[...] ニョロ語の動詞語根の声調パターンは 1 つで，不定形では原則パターン A で現れるが，これは動詞活用形で声調パターンがすべて A になるということではない。声調パターンが A，B のどちらになるかは，テンス・アスペクト・ムードごと，またその肯定・否定ごとに決まっている
tone.locator: Section 3 ニョロ語の声調, pp.63-64
tone.translation: The tone of Nyoro nominals has two patterns regardless of word length. (3) is a tonal minimal pair of nouns: pattern (3a) has an underlying high tone H on the second syllable from the end (called pattern A for convenience), and pattern (3b) has an underlying H on the last syllable (pattern B). [...] Nyoro verb roots have a single tone pattern and infinitives in principle appear in pattern A, but this does not mean all conjugated forms are A: whether a form is A or B is fixed per tense/aspect/mood and per affirmative/negative.
